title: The First Villagers
subtitle: Ohalo II, the Natufians and the first bread
summary: Long before farming, foragers in the Levant ground wild cereals at Ohalo II, and the Natufians built stone houses, baked bread, feasted and buried their dead beneath their floors. Whether the Younger Dryas pushed them towards cultivation is still debated.
narration: In 1989 a drought lowered the Sea of Galilee, and on its exposed shore archaeologists found the charred remains of six brush huts. The camp, called Ohalo II, had burned and then been drowned about 23,000 years ago, and the water had preserved almost everything: grass bedding on a hut floor, a grinding stone with traces of wild barley and wheat, flint blades polished by cutting cereal stalks, and seeds and fruits from about 140 kinds of plant.

Eight thousand years later, in the same region, people did something new. The Natufians, who lived in the Levant between about 15,000 and 11,600 years ago, built round stone houses and stayed in them for much of the year. They harvested wild cereals with bone-handled sickles, pounded food in mortars cut into bedrock, and buried their dead beneath their floors, sometimes with dogs. At Shubayqa in the Jordanian desert, charred crumbs show that people were baking a kind of flatbread 14,400 years ago, some 4,000 years before farming.

They held feasts and honoured unusual people. In a small cave in Galilee, a woman with a twisted spine was buried about 12,000 years ago with 50 tortoise shells, the wing of an eagle and the foot of another person.

Then came the cold, dry centuries of the Younger Dryas. Some archaeologists think hardship pushed these foragers to start cultivating; others think they simply moved around more. Either way, their genomes show that they were ancestors of the region’s first farmers.

body.heading: Ohalo II: a camp by the lake
paragraphs: In 1989 a drought exposed the remains of a camp on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Excavated by Dani Nadel of the University of Haifa in 1989–91 and again when the water fell in 1999–2001, Ohalo II had burned and then been sealed by rising water and silt around 23,000 years ago, preserving plant remains that rarely survive. There were six oval huts of brushwood; the floor of one was lined with bundles of grass, the oldest known bedding. A man was buried nearby.

Ehud Weiss and colleagues identified tens of thousands of seeds and fruits from about 140 plant species, including wild barley, wild emmer wheat, wild oats, figs, grapes, olives and many small-seeded grasses. Starch grains of barley and wheat on a flat basalt stone showed that grain was being ground (Dolores Piperno and colleagues, 2004), and a 2016 study led by Iris Groman-Yaroslavski found flint blades with the gloss typical of harvesting cereal stems. In 2015 Ainit Snir, Weiss and colleagues argued that 13 species of plants typical of arable weeds, found among the cereals, point to small-scale trial cultivation some 11,000 years before farming took hold. Critics reply that such plants also grow on naturally disturbed ground and could have been gathered with the grain. The inhabitants also fished in the lake and hunted gazelle, deer and birds.

body.heading: Kebaran foragers
paragraphs: Ohalo II belongs to the early Epipalaeolithic of the Levant. The Kebaran culture, named after Kebara Cave on Mount Carmel, lasted from about 23,000 to 17,500 years ago and is known for tiny bladelets; the Geometric Kebaran, from about 17,500 to 15,000 years ago, added trapezes and rectangles, standardised inserts for composite tools. Most groups moved seasonally between the lowlands and the hills. Some places drew larger gatherings: at Kharaneh IV in the Jordanian steppe, Lisa Maher’s team found hut floors, burials and thousands of shell beads, some from the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, at a site occupied around 19,800–18,600 years ago, suggesting that people from wide areas came together there.

body.heading: The Natufians settle down
paragraphs: The Natufian culture was named by Dorothy Garrod after Wadi en-Natuf, where she excavated Shuqba Cave in 1928. It spans about 15,000–11,600 years ago and is usually divided into Early, Late and Final phases. Early Natufian sites in the Mediterranean woodland of the southern Levant show a new way of life: semi-subterranean round houses with stone walls, hearths and storage, used for much of the year. At ʿAin Mallaha (Eynan) in the Hula Valley, excavated by Jean Perrot from 1955 and later by François Valla, houses up to about 9 metres across cluster on a slope, and the dead were buried among and beneath them, including a woman with a puppy (chapter 24). At el-Wad on Mount Carmel, Garrod found burials with elaborate headdresses of dentalium shells, and at Hayonim Cave in Galilee, Ofer Bar-Yosef’s team found round rooms and a grave in which people had been buried with two dogs.

Staying put changed the neighbours. A 2017 study led by Lior Weissbrod showed that house mice outcompeted wild mice at Natufian sites, the first known commensal house mice. Natufians hunted gazelle intensively, along with deer, wild boar, hares and birds, and processed plant foods on a scale not seen before.

body.heading: Sickles, mortars and the first bread
paragraphs: The Natufian toolkit was geared to plants. Flint blades set in straight bone handles, some carved at the end with animal heads, served as sickles, and their edges carry the gloss of cutting stems. Mortars were carved into bedrock or boulders, some deep and narrow, alongside pestles, basalt bowls and grinding slabs. At Shubayqa 1 in the basalt desert of northeastern Jordan, Amaia Arranz-Otaegui, Tobias Richter and colleagues reported in 2018 charred fragments of bread-like food, about 14,400 years old, made from ground wild cereals such as einkorn, barley or oats mixed with tubers of club-rush. It is the oldest known bread, about 4,000 years older than farming. The authors suggest that bread, laborious to make, may have been a special food whose appeal later encouraged cultivation.

At Raqefet Cave on Mount Carmel, where Dani Nadel’s team found graves lined with flowering plants such as sage and mint, a 2018 study led by Li Liu analysed residues in bedrock mortars about 13,000 years old. Starch grains with damage typical of malting and mashing led the team to propose that Natufians brewed a thin, porridge-like beer from wheat or barley, perhaps for funeral feasts. Other researchers questioned whether the starch damage demonstrates fermentation and noted that open mortars are easily contaminated.

body.heading: Feasts, a shaman and lovers
paragraphs: Natufian ritual left striking traces. At Hilazon Tachtit, a small cave in western Galilee, Leore Grosman and colleagues found the grave of a woman aged about 45, buried about 12,000 years ago. A deformed pelvis and spine would have given her an uneven gait. The grave was lined and covered with stones and held 50 complete tortoise shells, the wing of an eagle, the pelvis of a leopard, the forearm of a wild boar, the tail of an aurochs, the skulls of two martens and a human foot. The excavators interpret her as a shaman, one of the earliest known. A nearby pit held remains of at least 71 tortoises and three aurochs, the leftovers of what Natalie Munro and Grosman (2010) describe as a funeral feast.

The ʿAin Sakhri lovers, a calcite pebble about 10 centimetres tall carved with a couple embracing, was found in a cave near Bethlehem and brought to scholarly attention by René Neuville in 1933. About 11,000 years old and now in the British Museum, it is often called the oldest known depiction of people making love.

body.heading: The Younger Dryas question
paragraphs: The Late Natufian, which overlaps with the Younger Dryas (about 12,900–11,700 years ago), looks different. Sites became smaller and more ephemeral, burials were more often secondary, and people ranged farther into the steppe and desert. Ofer Bar-Yosef and Anna Belfer-Cohen argued that the cold, dry Younger Dryas thinned the wild cereal stands on which Natufians had come to depend and pushed them to begin cultivating; Andrew Moore and Gordon Hillman made a similar case from Abu Hureyra. Critics, among them Lisa Maher, Ted Banning and Michael Chazan (2011), argue that local climate records do not show a simple crisis, that the Natufian response was to move more rather than to farm, and that domesticated cereals appear only much later, in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (chapter 33). Other explanations stress feasting, social competition and gradual niche construction.

Abu Hureyra on the Euphrates in Syria was excavated by Moore in 1972–73, before the Tabqa Dam flooded it beneath Lake Assad. Its Epipalaeolithic village preserved abundant plant remains. Hillman reported rye grains of domestic type about 13,000 years old, a claim many doubt because the grains are few and could be intrusive. In 2020 Moore, James Kennett and colleagues argued that melted glass and other markers show that the village was destroyed by a cosmic airburst about 12,800 years ago; critics argue that such glass forms when buildings and vegetation burn, and they reject the wider impact hypothesis (chapter 27).

body.heading: Natufian genomes
paragraphs: Hot climates destroy DNA, but in 2016 Iosif Lazaridis, David Reich and colleagues obtained genomes from Natufian burials at Raqefet Cave. The Natufians carried a large share of Basal Eurasian ancestry, a lineage that branched off early from other non-Africans and carries little Neanderthal DNA, and they were genetically close to the later Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of the southern Levant, supporting continuity from foragers to farmers. In 2018 genomes from Taforalt in Morocco, about 15,000 years old (chapter 26), turned out to share much of their ancestry with the Natufians, evidence of ancient connections between North Africa and the Levant whose direction is still debated.

debates.question: Did the people of Ohalo II cultivate cereals?

views.label: Trial cultivation
views.text: Ainit Snir, Ehud Weiss and colleagues (2015) argue that the mix of wild cereals with plants that today thrive as arable weeds, together with sickle blades and grinding stones, shows small-scale sowing some 23,000 years ago.

views.label: Intensive gathering
views.text: Sceptics note that the weed species also grow in natural disturbed habitats, such as lake shores, and that none of the cereals shows domestic traits, so intensive gathering explains the evidence equally well.

debates.status: Most researchers accept that Ohalo II shows sophisticated use of wild cereals; whether anything was sown remains unproven, and in any case the practice did not lead directly to farming.

debates.question: Did the Natufians brew beer?

views.label: Ritual brewing
views.text: Li Liu, Dani Nadel and colleagues (2018) argue that starch damage in Raqefet mortars matches malting, mashing and fermentation, and that beer was brewed for funerary feasts.

views.label: Not demonstrated
views.text: Critics argue that similar starch damage can result from other kinds of processing or from weathering, and that open bedrock mortars exposed for millennia are prone to contamination.

debates.status: The claim is plausible but not settled. Chemical markers of fermentation from securely sealed contexts would strengthen it.

debates.question: Did the Younger Dryas push people towards farming?

views.label: Climate as trigger
views.text: Ofer Bar-Yosef, Anna Belfer-Cohen, Andrew Moore and Gordon Hillman argued that cold and drought reduced wild cereals, prompting Natufians who had grown dependent on them to begin cultivating.

views.label: Other drivers
views.text: Lisa Maher, Ted Banning and Michael Chazan (2011), among others, find no simple crisis in local records and note that Late Natufians became more mobile; they and others emphasise social factors such as feasting and competition, and gradual niche construction.

debates.status: Most researchers now see the transition to farming as a long, regionally varied process in which climate mattered but did not act alone. Domesticated cereals appear only after the Younger Dryas (chapter 33).

debates.question: Was Abu Hureyra destroyed by a cosmic airburst?

views.label: Airburst
views.text: Andrew Moore, James Kennett and colleagues (2020) reported melted glass, nanodiamonds and microspherules in the layer dated about 12,800 years ago and attributed them to a comet airburst.

views.label: Ordinary fire
views.text: Critics argue that the glass formed when reed and mud-brick structures and vegetation burned, and that the other markers are not diagnostic of impacts.

debates.status: Few researchers outside the impact group accept the claim, which is tied to the widely rejected Younger Dryas impact hypothesis.

keyFacts.label: Ohalo II
keyFacts.value: About 23,000 years ago; about 140 plant species; the oldest known bedding

keyFacts.label: Natufian culture
keyFacts.value: About 15,000–11,600 years ago, southern and northern Levant

keyFacts.label: Hilazon Tachtit burial
keyFacts.value: About 12,000 years ago, with 50 tortoise shells

sites.name: Ohalo II
sites.summary: Drowned brush-hut camp on the Sea of Galilee with grass bedding, ground wild cereals, sickle blades and about 140 plant species.

sites.name: Kebara Cave
sites.summary: Mount Carmel cave that gave its name to the Kebaran culture; its Natufian layers yielded carved bone sickle hafts.

sites.name: Kharaneh IV
sites.summary: Large Epipalaeolithic aggregation site in the Jordanian steppe with hut floors, burials and shell beads from two seas.

sites.name: ʿAin Mallaha (Eynan)
sites.summary: Natufian village of round, stone-walled houses in the Hula Valley, with burials beneath the floors, including a woman with a puppy.

sites.name: el-Wad
sites.summary: Mount Carmel cave and terrace where Dorothy Garrod found Natufian burials with dentalium-shell headdresses.

sites.name: Hayonim Cave
sites.summary: Galilee cave with Natufian round rooms and a grave in which people were buried with two dogs.

sites.name: Raqefet Cave
sites.summary: Natufian cemetery with flower-lined graves, mortars proposed as beer-brewing vessels, and the source of the first Natufian genomes.

sites.name: Shubayqa 1
sites.summary: Natufian site in the basalt desert whose hearth held charred bread-like remains, the oldest known bread.

sites.name: Hilazon Tachtit
sites.summary: Small cave with the burial of a woman interpreted as a shaman, accompanied by 50 tortoise shells and animal parts, and remains of a feast.

sites.name: ʿAin Sakhri
sites.summary: Cave near Bethlehem that yielded the ʿAin Sakhri lovers figurine, a carved pebble showing a couple embracing.

sites.name: Abu Hureyra
sites.dateLabel: Epipalaeolithic village from about 13,400 years ago
sites.summary: Euphrates village, now under Lake Assad, with rich plant remains, a contested claim of early rye cultivation and a disputed airburst claim.
